q: The apron of a centre lathe is the assembly which:

options.A: Houses the main spindle and the speed-change gearing of the lathe
options.B: Is fitted to the front of the carriage, travels with it along the bed and houses the feed mechanism and the half-nuts which engage the lead screw for thread cutting
options.C: Supports the outer end of a long workpiece held between centres
options.D: Carries the grinding attachment used for finishing the workpiece

e: The apron is mounted on the front of the lathe carriage and moves with it along the bed; it houses the feed mechanism and the half-nuts that engage the lead screw, so thread cutting and power feeds are both operated from the apron.

q: The back-gear arrangement provided in the headstock of a centre lathe serves mainly to:

options.A: Reverse the direction of rotation of the spindle for cutting left-hand threads
options.B: Connect the spindle directly to the motor for the highest speeds
options.C: Provide a range of reduced spindle speeds with increased turning effort, for heavy cuts and large-diameter work
options.D: Drive the lead screw independently of the spindle

e: Back gears in the headstock give a geared reduction between the cone pulley and the spindle, producing low spindle speeds with high torque, which standard lathe practice reserves for heavy cuts and large-diameter work.

q: A revolving (live) centre fitted in the tailstock of a lathe differs from an ordinary dead centre in that the live centre:

options.A: Rotates with the workpiece on its own bearings, so that friction and heating at the centre are greatly reduced
options.B: Is fixed rigidly in the headstock and drives the workpiece round
options.C: Is used only for holding work in a chuck and never between centres
options.D: Is made of soft metal which wears away instead of the workpiece

e: A revolving centre turns in the tailstock on its own bearings and rotates with the workpiece, unlike a dead centre which stays stationary; this greatly reduces friction, wear and heating at the centre hole.

q: Long tapers on work held between the centres of a lathe are turned by the tailstock set-over method, in which:

options.A: The tool is fed at an angle by means of the compound slide
options.B: The workpiece is held in a chuck and the tool is set at half the taper angle
options.C: A tapered guide bar controls the movement of the tool along the work
options.D: The tailstock body is shifted sideways from the lathe axis, so that the workpiece is inclined to the axis and a taper is produced as the tool travels parallel to the bed

e: In tailstock set-over, the tailstock body is offset sideways so the work axis is inclined to the lathe axis while the tool travels parallel to the bed; the diameter then varies uniformly along the length, producing a long taper.

q: The knee of a column-and-knee type milling machine is the part which:

options.A: Supports the outer end of the cutter arbor
options.B: Slides vertically on the face of the column and carries the saddle and the table, so that the work can be raised or lowered in relation to the cutter
options.C: Houses the spindle and the speed-change gearing of the machine
options.D: Clamps the workpiece directly and indexes it for gear cutting

e: The knee of a column-and-knee milling machine slides vertically on the column face and carries the saddle and table; raising or lowering the knee sets the work height relative to the cutter, as per standard machine construction.

q: A planing machine (planer) installed in a workshop differs from a shaping machine mainly in that, on the planer:

options.A: The work table carrying the job reciprocates past a stationary tool, the machine being suited to large and heavy work requiring flat surfaces
options.B: The tool reciprocates over a stationary job, the machine being suited only to small work
options.C: The cutter rotates continuously while the job is fed slowly under it
options.D: The job is rotated between centres while the tool is fed along it

e: On a planer the table carrying the job reciprocates past a stationary tool held in the clapper head, whereas on a shaper the tool reciprocates over a fixed job; the planer arrangement suits large, heavy work needing flat surfaces.

q: The 'swing' specified for a centre lathe indicates:

options.A: The length of the bed of the lathe between the headstock and the tailstock
options.B: The distance which the carriage can travel along the bed
options.C: The largest diameter of work which can be turned over the bed of the lathe, and thus the size of work the lathe can accommodate
options.D: The range through which the compound slide can be swivelled

e: Swing is the maximum diameter of work that can be rotated over the lathe bed without fouling it; it is the standard specification that fixes the size of work a centre lathe can accommodate.

q: On a CNC machine tool installed in a workshop, the movements of the tool and the work are controlled by:

options.A: The operator moving the hand wheels in a fixed sequence for every component
options.B: A set of cams and stops which the operator resets for every component
options.C: Hydraulic copying from a template placed beside the machine
options.D: A stored programme of instructions, the machine executing the programmed sequence of movements automatically, component after component

e: CNC control stores the machining instructions as a programme and the control system executes the programmed tool and work movements automatically in sequence, repeating the cycle component after component without manual hand-wheel operation.

q: A machine vice, as used in the machine shops of a workshop, is a work-holding device which:

options.A: Is mounted on the table of a machine such as a milling or drilling machine and holds the workpiece for machining, the vice often having a swivelling base for setting the work at an angle
options.B: Is fixed permanently on the fitter's bench and is used only for hand filing and sawing
options.C: Grips pipes and round bars only, by means of a chain
options.D: Holds the cutting tool of the machine in position during the cut

e: A machine vice is bolted to the table of a milling, drilling or similar machine to grip the workpiece during machining; many have a swivelling base so the work can also be set at an angle to the cutter.

q: Work too large or irregular to be held in a machine vice is clamped directly on the machine table mainly by means of:

options.A: A magnetic chuck fitted over the whole table
options.B: Strap clamps, in which a flat strap presses on the work and is tightened by a stud or bolt engaging the table slots, with a packing block supporting the other end of the strap
options.C: A collet drawn into the spindle of the machine
options.D: Centres fitted at the two ends of the table

e: Work too large or irregular for a vice is held by strap clamps: a flat strap bears on the work, a stud or bolt in a table T-slot tightens it, and a packing block of work height supports the free end of the strap.

q: The three-wire method is employed in the inspection section of a workshop for:

options.A: Checking the flatness of a surface plate at three points
options.B: Measuring the bore of a cylinder at three positions along its length
options.C: Setting the three jaws of a self-centring chuck truly concentric
options.D: Accurately measuring the effective (pitch) diameter of an external screw thread, wires being placed in the thread grooves and the measurement taken over the wires

e: In the three-wire method, wires of known diameter rest in the thread grooves and the dimension over the wires is measured with a micrometer; from this the effective or pitch diameter of an external thread is calculated accurately.

q: Grey cast iron, widely used in a workshop for machine beds, bases and frames, is characterised by:

options.A: Its carbon being present wholly in the combined form, making it extremely hard and unmachinable
options.B: Its containing no carbon at all, being a pure form of iron
options.C: Its carbon being present largely as flakes of graphite, which give it good vibration-damping capacity and easy machinability, though it is brittle in tension
options.D: Its being a non-ferrous alloy of copper and zinc

e: In grey cast iron most carbon exists as graphite flakes; the flakes make it easy to machine and give excellent vibration damping for beds and frames, but they also make the iron weak and brittle in tension.

q: Malleable cast iron, used in a workshop for fittings and components which must withstand shock, is produced by:

options.A: Adding a large quantity of zinc to molten cast iron in the cupola
options.B: Heat-treating castings made of white cast iron, whereby the castings gain ductility and toughness instead of the brittleness of ordinary cast iron
options.C: Forging ordinary grey cast iron castings under a power hammer
options.D: Slowly cooling steel castings in the mould itself

e: Malleable cast iron is made by prolonged heat treatment of white cast iron castings; the treatment breaks down the brittle carbide into free carbon nodules, giving the castings ductility and shock resistance.

q: Gunmetal, used in a workshop for bearings, bushes and pump and valve parts, is an alloy consisting essentially of:

options.A: Copper, tin and zinc
options.B: Iron, carbon and manganese
options.C: Aluminium, copper and magnesium
options.D: Lead, tin and antimony

e: Gunmetal is a bronze alloy of copper, tin and zinc, valued for corrosion resistance and bearing properties, and is standard workshop material for bushes, bearings and pump and valve parts.

q: Duralumin, as a material handled in a workshop, is:

options.A: A variety of cast iron used for heavy machine frames
options.B: A hard grade of tool steel used for lathe tools
options.C: A copper alloy used for bearings and bushes
options.D: A light alloy based on aluminium, which combines lightness with considerable strength and is used for sheet and structural work

e: Duralumin is an aluminium-based light alloy with copper and other additions; after heat treatment it combines low weight with strength approaching mild steel, suiting it to sheet and structural work.

q: Martensite, as the term is used in the heat treatment of steel in a workshop, is:

options.A: The soft constituent of steel which forms on very slow cooling
options.B: A coating of oxide formed on steel during heating in the furnace
options.C: The hard, needle-like constituent formed when steel is cooled rapidly by quenching, to which the hardness of quenched steel is mainly due
options.D: The slag which separates from steel in the melting furnace

e: Martensite is the hard, needle-like structure formed when austenite is cooled rapidly by quenching so that carbon cannot escape; the hardness of quenched steel is mainly due to this trapped, distorted structure.

q: A bend test carried out on a specimen of material or on a welded joint in a workshop consists of:

options.A: Pulling the specimen in a testing machine until it breaks
options.B: Bending the specimen, and examining the outer surface of the bend for cracks, so as to judge the ductility and soundness of the material or the weld
options.C: Striking the specimen with a swinging pendulum and measuring the energy absorbed
options.D: Pressing a hardened ball into the specimen and measuring the impression

e: In a bend test the specimen is bent through a specified angle and the outer, stretched surface is examined for cracks; freedom from cracking shows adequate ductility and, for a weld, soundness of the joint.

q: In the Izod impact test carried out on a material specimen in a workshop:

options.A: A notched specimen is clamped vertically in a vice as a cantilever, with the notch facing the striker, and is broken by a single blow of a swinging pendulum
options.B: A notched specimen is supported horizontally at its two ends and struck in the middle, opposite the notch
options.C: The specimen is twisted until it fails and the angle of twist is recorded
options.D: The specimen is compressed between two flat plates until it crushes

e: In the Izod test a notched specimen is clamped vertically as a cantilever with the notch facing the striker and is broken by one pendulum blow; the energy absorbed, read from the pendulum swing, measures impact toughness.

q: The endurance (fatigue) limit of a metal, as the term is used in connection with workshop components, means:

options.A: The maximum load which a component can bear once, without breaking
options.B: The temperature up to which a component can be heated without softening
options.C: The number of years for which a component can be kept in stock
options.D: The stress level below which the metal can withstand an indefinitely large number of repeated stress cycles without failing by fatigue

e: The endurance or fatigue limit is the stress below which a metal can endure an indefinitely large number of repeated stress cycles without fatigue failure; above it, life is finite and falls as stress rises.

q: The clearance angle provided on a single-point cutting tool used in a workshop is the angle:

options.A: Of inclination of the top face of the tool, over which the chip slides
options.B: Included between the two cutting edges of a twist drill
options.C: Between the flank of the tool and the surface of the work, provided so that the flank does not rub on the work and only the cutting edge engages it
options.D: At which the tool is set in the tool post in relation to the work axis

e: The clearance angle lies between the tool flank and the machined surface and exists so only the cutting edge contacts the work; without it the flank would rub, generating heat and a poor finish.

q: The nose of a single-point lathe tool is given a small radius mainly in order to:

options.A: Make the tool suitable for cutting screw threads of all pitches
options.B: Strengthen the tip of the tool and improve the surface finish of the work, a sharp pointed tip being weak and leaving feed marks
options.C: Allow the tool to cut in both directions of travel of the carriage
options.D: Reduce the height at which the tool must be set in the tool post

e: A small nose radius strengthens the tool tip, which would otherwise be a weak sharp point liable to chip, and it smooths out feed marks, giving a better surface finish on the work.

q: A form tool, as used on a lathe in a workshop, is a cutting tool which:

options.A: Has its cutting edge ground to the exact profile to be produced, so that the required shape is reproduced on the work in a single plunge or traverse cut
options.B: Is forged by the smith to a rough shape and finished by the fitter before use
options.C: Is used only for cutting off finished work from the bar
options.D: Changes its shape automatically to suit each job taken up

e: A form tool has its cutting edge ground to the exact profile required, so one plunge or traverse cut reproduces that profile on the work, as used for radii, grooves and special shapes on lathes.

q: A built-up edge formed on a cutting tool during machining in a workshop consists of:

options.A: A layer of grinding dust deposited on the tool during sharpening
options.B: A protective coating applied to the tool before it is put to work
options.C: The hardened skin formed on the workpiece by the previous cut
options.D: Fragments of the work material which, under the pressure and heat of cutting, weld themselves to the face and edge of the tool and break away from time to time, spoiling the finish of the work

e: A built-up edge is work material pressure-welded to the tool face and edge by cutting heat and pressure; it grows and breaks away periodically, the fragments scoring the work and spoiling finish and size.

q: When a brittle material such as cast iron is machined in a workshop, the chips produced are generally:

options.A: Long continuous ribbons which coil away from the tool
options.B: A fine powder produced only when the tool is completely blunt
options.C: Discontinuous, breaking into separate segments, because the material cannot undergo much deformation before fracturing
options.D: Molten droplets which solidify after falling from the tool

e: Brittle materials like cast iron cannot deform much before fracturing, so the chip breaks into short discontinuous segments instead of forming the long continuous ribbons typical of ductile metals.

q: A grinding wheel in use in a workshop is said to be loaded when:

options.A: Its abrasive grains have become dull and shiny and have ceased to cut
options.B: Metal particles from the work have become clogged in the spaces between the grains of its face, so that the wheel cuts poorly and tends to heat the work
options.C: It has been mounted on the spindle with an excessive load of workpieces beside it
options.D: It has cracked across its face and become unfit for use

e: A loaded wheel has metal particles clogged in the pores between its abrasive grains; the face then rubs rather than cuts, causing poor cutting, glazing of the work and excessive heating.

q: Before a grinding wheel is mounted on its spindle in a workshop, it is commonly subjected to a ring test, in which:

options.A: The suspended wheel is tapped lightly and a clear ringing tone indicates a sound wheel, while a dull sound indicates a cracked wheel which must be rejected
options.B: The wheel is rotated at full speed for a fixed period and its temperature is noted
options.C: A ring gauge is passed over the bore of the wheel to check its size
options.D: The wheel is immersed in water and watched for air bubbles

e: In the ring test a suspended wheel is tapped lightly; a clear ringing tone shows a sound wheel, while a dull thud indicates a crack, and standard grinding safety practice requires such a wheel to be rejected.

q: A spur gear, as used in the drives of workshop machines, is a gear:

options.A: Whose teeth are cut at an angle to its axis, giving a gradual and quiet engagement
options.B: Whose teeth are cut on a tapered blank for transmitting motion between inclined shafts
options.C: Which meshes with a straight toothed bar to convert rotary motion into linear motion
options.D: Whose teeth are straight and parallel to its axis, transmitting motion between parallel shafts in the simplest form of gearing

e: A spur gear has straight teeth cut parallel to its axis and meshes with another spur gear on a parallel shaft; it is the simplest gear form, used widely in workshop machine drives.

q: A helical gear differs from a spur gear in that, in the helical gear:

options.A: The teeth are cut on the inside of a ring instead of on the outside
options.B: There are no teeth, motion being transmitted by friction alone
options.C: The teeth are inclined to the axis of the gear, so that engagement is gradual, the drive is smoother and quieter, and an end thrust is produced along the shaft
options.D: The gear is always made of cast iron and never of steel

e: Helical gear teeth are cut at an angle to the axis, so teeth engage gradually and more than one tooth shares the load, giving smoother, quieter running; the inclination also produces axial end thrust on the shaft.

q: A rack and pinion arrangement, as used in workshop machines, consists of:

options.A: Two toothed wheels of very different sizes meshing with each other
options.B: A pinion meshing with a straight bar in which teeth are cut, the arrangement converting rotary motion into straight-line motion, or the reverse
options.C: A toothed belt running over two pulleys of equal size
options.D: A worm meshing with a worm wheel at right angles

e: A rack is a straight bar with gear teeth cut in it; a pinion meshing with it converts rotary motion into straight-line motion or the reverse, as in the traverse drives of workshop machines.

q: The module of a gear, by which the size of its teeth is expressed, is:

options.A: The ratio of the pitch-circle diameter of the gear to the number of its teeth, gears which are to mesh together having the same module
options.B: The whole depth of the tooth measured from its tip to its root
options.C: The distance between the centres of two gears in mesh
options.D: The number of teeth which the gear carries on its rim

e: Module is the pitch-circle diameter divided by the number of teeth, in millimetres; it expresses tooth size, and gears that mesh together must have the same module.

q: A chain drive, as used for transmitting power between shafts in a workshop, has the advantage over a belt drive that:

options.A: It requires no lubrication of any kind throughout its life
options.B: It can transmit motion even when the chain is slack and worn out
options.C: It is completely silent at all speeds of working
options.D: It is a positive drive without slip, the chain engaging the toothed sprockets, so that an exact speed ratio is maintained

e: A chain engages the teeth of its sprockets positively, so there is no slip and the speed ratio stays exact; this is the chief advantage of a chain drive over a friction belt drive.

q: A V-belt drive is preferred to a flat-belt drive for short centre distances in workshop machines mainly because:

options.A: The V-belt runs in grooves without touching the pulley at all
options.B: The V-belt is made of leather and lasts longer than any flat belt
options.C: The V-section of the belt wedges into the grooved pulley, giving a firm grip with little slip, so that the drive is compact and can transmit considerable power over a short distance
options.D: The V-belt requires a much larger pulley than a flat belt for the same work

e: The V-belt wedges into the grooved pulley, and the wedging action multiplies the grip, so a V-belt transmits considerable power with little slip over short centre distances in a compact drive.

q: A roller bearing fitted in workshop machinery differs from a ball bearing in that the roller bearing:

options.A: Uses cylindrical rollers between its races, the line contact so obtained enabling it to carry heavier radial loads than a ball bearing of comparable size
options.B: Uses no rolling elements at all, the shaft sliding directly on the housing
options.C: Can carry only end loads along the shaft and no load across it
options.D: Is filled with molten metal which solidifies around the shaft

e: Roller bearings use cylindrical rollers giving line contact with the races, instead of the point contact of balls; line contact carries heavier radial loads for a bearing of comparable size.

q: A thrust bearing fitted to a shaft in workshop machinery is a bearing designed mainly to:

options.A: Support the radial weight of a horizontal shaft at its journals
options.B: Take the end load acting along the axis of the shaft, as with a vertical shaft or a shaft subject to axial pressure
options.C: Hold the lubricant in place around an ordinary journal bearing
options.D: Prevent dust from entering an ordinary ball bearing

e: A thrust bearing is designed to resist loads acting along the shaft axis, such as the weight of a vertical shaft or axial pressure, which ordinary journal bearings are not meant to carry.

q: A flange coupling, as used to join two shafts in a workshop machine drive, consists of:

options.A: A sleeve of rubber slipped over the two shaft ends
options.B: A pair of toothed wheels connected by an endless chain
options.C: A loose belt connecting two pulleys on the shaft ends
options.D: Two flanged discs, each keyed to a shaft end and bolted face to face, forming a rigid coupling suited to shafts held in accurate alignment

e: A flange coupling has two flanged discs, each keyed to one shaft end, bolted face to face; it forms a rigid joint and therefore requires the two shafts to be in accurate alignment.

q: A Woodruff key, used in assembling a wheel or pulley on a shaft in a workshop, is a key which:

options.A: Is driven into a tapered hole drilled half in the shaft and half in the hub
options.B: Is a plain parallel bar sunk equally into the shaft and the hub
options.C: Is segmental in shape, fitting into a semicircular pocket milled in the shaft, and can tilt so as to align itself with the keyway in the hub
options.D: Is screwed into the hub and bears on a flat on the shaft

e: A Woodruff key is a segment of a disc seated in a semicircular pocket milled in the shaft; it can tilt in its pocket to align itself with the hub keyway, which is its special advantage.

q: A spring washer placed under a nut in a workshop assembly serves mainly to:

options.A: Exert a spring pressure on the nut after tightening, so that the nut is resisted from slackening back under vibration
options.B: Increase the bearing area of the nut on a soft surface
options.C: Seal the joint against the leakage of oil or water
options.D: Insulate the bolted joint electrically from the machine body

e: A spring washer is compressed flat on tightening and keeps exerting spring pressure on the nut, maintaining friction in the threads so the nut resists slackening under vibration.

q: A stud, as a fastening used in workshop assemblies, is:

options.A: A bolt with an enlarged head used only for foundation work
options.B: A metal rod threaded at both ends and having no head, one end being screwed into a tapped hole in the component and the other end receiving a nut, as used for covers and joints which are opened frequently
options.C: A pin driven through a nut and bolt to lock them together
options.D: A screw which is threaded along its whole length and has a head for a spanner

e: A stud is threaded at both ends with no head; one end screws permanently into a tapped hole in the component and the other takes a nut, suiting covers and joints that are opened frequently.

q: Shims, as used in the erection and maintenance work of a workshop, are:

options.A: Wedges used to split castings in the foundry
options.B: Abrasive strips used to polish the journals of shafts
options.C: Gauges used to measure the clearance between gear teeth
options.D: Thin pieces of metal sheet or strip inserted under a machine or a bearing part to adjust its height, level or alignment

e: Shims are thin strips of metal sheet inserted under a machine foot or bearing part; adding or removing them adjusts height, level and alignment precisely during erection and maintenance.

q: The activity ratio used in standard costing in a workshop is the ratio of:

options.A: The actual hours worked to the hours of attendance recorded at the gate
options.B: The direct wages paid to the standard wages allowed for the outturn
options.C: The standard hours produced in the outturn of a period to the budgeted hours for that period, showing how the hours available were utilised in producing work
options.D: The on-cost absorbed on jobs to the actual on-cost incurred

e: The activity ratio in standard costing is standard hours produced divided by budgeted hours, expressed as a percentage; it shows how much useful work was produced from the hours budgeted for the period.

q: The capacity ratio used in standard costing in a workshop is the ratio of:

options.A: The actual hours worked in a period to the budgeted hours for that period, showing the extent to which the budgeted capacity was actually worked
options.B: The standard hours produced to the actual hours worked
options.C: The machine hours worked to the direct labour hours booked
options.D: The outturn transferred to the expenditure booked during the period

e: The capacity ratio is actual hours worked divided by budgeted hours; it shows the extent to which the budgeted capacity of the workshop was actually worked in the period.

q: In costing, an imputed cost is a cost which:

options.A: Has been paid in cash to an outside party during the period
options.B: Is recognised for costing and decision purposes although no actual payment is made for it, as in the case of interest on capital provided by the undertaking itself
options.C: Arises only from the use of material drawn from the stores depot
options.D: Is charged to jobs only when the outturn is transferred to stores

e: An imputed cost is recognised in cost accounts for decision and comparison purposes although no cash is paid, the standard example being interest on capital provided by the undertaking itself.

q: Service costing (operating costing), as a method of costing, is the method applied where:

options.A: Each job is separately identifiable and is executed against a specific work order
options.B: Production flows continuously through a sequence of processes
options.C: A single standard product is manufactured in large quantities over a long period
options.D: Services are rendered, the cost being ascertained for a period and expressed per unit of service rendered

e: Service or operating costing applies where services rather than goods are rendered; costs are collected for a period and expressed per unit of service, such as per vehicle-kilometre or per passenger carried.

q: A flexible budget, as used for the control of workshop overheads, is a budget which:

options.A: Once prepared, is never altered for the whole of its period
options.B: Provides only for the fixed expenses of the workshop and ignores variable expenses
options.C: Is recast to the level of activity actually attained, by recognising the fixed and variable behaviour of expenses, so that actual performance can be compared with the budget for that level
options.D: Is prepared separately for every individual job undertaken in the workshop

e: A flexible budget is recast for the level of activity actually attained, separating fixed costs, which stay constant, from variable costs, which change with activity, so actuals are compared with a fair budget for that level.

q: Obsolescence of machinery and plant in a workshop means that the machine:

options.A: Loses its usefulness and value because improved designs or methods have made it out of date, although it may still be in a physically serviceable condition
options.B: Is worn out by constant use and can no longer be run at all
options.C: Is damaged in an accident and has to be repaired before use
options.D: Is kept idle for want of work in the shop for a short period

e: Obsolescence is loss of usefulness and value because improved designs or methods have made a machine out of date; the machine may still be physically serviceable, unlike one that is simply worn out.

q: Buffing, as carried out on a manufactured component in a workshop, is a finishing process in which the surface is:

options.A: Ground with a coarse revolving wheel to remove surplus metal rapidly
options.B: Polished on a revolving soft cloth wheel charged with a fine abrasive compound, to give it a bright and lustrous finish
options.C: Coated with zinc by dipping it in a bath of molten metal
options.D: Cleaned by immersing it in an acid bath to remove scale and rust

e: Buffing polishes a surface on a revolving soft cloth mop charged with a fine abrasive compound; it removes no appreciable metal and produces the bright, lustrous finish required on plated and decorative work.

q: In the machine shops of a workshop, the term 'swarf' means:

options.A: The chips, turnings and filings removed from a workpiece during machining
options.B: The slag that floats on the surface of molten metal in a furnace
options.C: The sand that remains clinging to a casting after it is taken out of the mould
options.D: The dust collected from the floors of the shops at the end of a shift

e: Swarf is the collective term for the chips, turnings, borings and filings cut from workpieces during machining, collected in the machine shops for disposal or sale as scrap.

q: Drifting, as carried out on a holed component in a workshop, consists of:

options.A: Drilling a fresh hole in the component at a marked position
options.B: Cutting an internal screw thread inside an existing hole
options.C: Driving a tapered drift through a hole to enlarge it and to bring it into true alignment or size
options.D: Bending a bar gradually to a required curvature over a former

e: Drifting drives a tapered drift through an existing hole, enlarging it slightly and bringing it into true size and alignment, commonly to align holes in mating parts for riveting or bolting.

q: A bore gauge used in the inspection section of a workshop is an instrument employed mainly for:

options.A: Measuring the outside diameter of a shaft or pin
options.B: Measuring the depth of a blind hole from its face
options.C: Checking the pitch of a screw thread cut on a bolt
options.D: Measuring the internal size of holes and bores accurately, by comparison with a standard

e: A bore gauge measures internal diameters by comparison with a standard such as a micrometer or ring gauge; it is the inspection instrument for checking holes and bores accurately.

q: A telescopic gauge used in a workshop is a small internal measuring gauge which:

options.A: Has spring-loaded plungers that expand to the size of a bore and are locked there, the size then being measured with a micrometer
options.B: Reads the size of a bore directly from a graduated scale engraved on its stem
options.C: Measures the angle to which the bore of a component is inclined
options.D: Checks only whether a hole is larger or smaller than a fixed standard size

e: A telescopic gauge has spring-loaded plungers that expand to touch the bore walls and are then locked; withdrawn from the bore, the locked size is measured with a micrometer to get the internal dimension.

q: A dot punch used by a fitter in marking out work in a workshop is a punch which:

options.A: Is used for driving pins out of their holes during dismantling
options.B: Makes the deep conical mark at which a drill is started on a component
options.C: Has a fine sharp point and is used to mark scribed lines with a series of small dots, so that the layout remains visible during machining
options.D: Is used for cutting a circular blank out of a sheet of metal

e: A dot punch has a fine sharp point and is used to mark scribed layout lines with a series of small dots or witness marks, so the marking-out remains visible even after machining begins.

q: A trammel (beam compass) used in the fitting shop of a workshop is an instrument employed for:

options.A: Scribing lines parallel to the edge of a plate at a set distance
options.B: Scribing or measuring large circles and arcs which are beyond the reach of ordinary dividers
options.C: Checking that two faces of a component are truly at right angles
options.D: Measuring the thickness of a sheet of metal at its edge

e: A trammel or beam compass carries its points on a long beam, extending its reach far beyond ordinary dividers; it is used for scribing and measuring large circles and arcs in layout work.

q: An inside caliper used in a workshop is a measuring instrument whose legs:

options.A: Are straight and pointed, and are used for transferring a length from a rule
options.B: Carry a graduated scale from which the size is read off directly
options.C: Are hinged to a dial which indicates the size being measured
options.D: Curve outwards at their tips, so that the instrument can measure internal diameters and other inside dimensions

e: An inside caliper has legs that curve outwards at the tips, so the tips can enter a bore and contact its walls; the setting is then transferred to a rule or micrometer to read the internal size.

q: A file card used by fitters in a workshop is:

options.A: A brush of short fine wire bristles used for cleaning the teeth of a file
options.B: A card on which the files issued to a worker are recorded
options.C: A coarse file used for the first rough shaping of a component
options.D: A holder in which a broken piece of file is fixed for use

e: A file card is a brush of short fine wire bristles drawn across a file to clear metal particles clogged between its teeth, restoring the file's clean cutting action.

q: Draw filing, as practised in the fitting shop of a workshop, is the method of filing in which the file is:

options.A: Pushed forward in a straight line across the width of the work only
options.B: Held by both hands across the work and pushed and pulled along its length, to produce a smooth flat finish and remove earlier file marks
options.C: Worked round the edge of a circular component to round it off
options.D: Used with a reciprocating motion in a filing machine for production work

e: In draw filing the file is held by both hands across the work and pushed and pulled along its length; this shearing action removes earlier cross file marks and leaves a smooth, flat, finished surface.

q: A file used in a workshop is said to be 'pinned' when:

options.A: Its handle has been driven firmly on to the tang of the file
options.B: It has been fixed in a vice for use as a stationary tool
options.C: Its teeth have been sharpened afresh on a grinding wheel
options.D: Particles of metal have become lodged and clogged between its teeth, so that it scratches the work and ceases to cut cleanly

e: A file is pinned when particles of the metal being filed lodge between its teeth; the lodged particles scratch the work surface and the file skates instead of cutting cleanly.

q: A rasp used in the fitting shop of a workshop is a file-like tool whose distinguishing feature is that:

options.A: Its teeth are cut in two sets of parallel grooves crossing each other
options.B: It has no teeth at all and works only by the abrasive coating on its face
options.C: Its teeth are raised individually by a punch, making it a coarse tool suited to rough work on soft materials
options.D: Its blade is flexible and is used in a frame like a saw

e: A rasp has its teeth raised individually by a punch, standing as separate coarse points; this makes it an aggressive tool suited to rough shaping of soft materials like wood, leather and soft metal.

q: Straddle milling, as carried out on a milling machine in a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Milling two parallel faces of a workpiece at the same time with two side milling cutters mounted on the same arbor and spaced apart
options.B: Milling a flat surface with a large-diameter cutter mounted on the machine spindle
options.C: Milling the teeth of a gear with a formed cutter on a dividing head
options.D: Milling a long workpiece in two separate settings from opposite ends

e: Straddle milling mounts two side milling cutters on one arbor, spaced to the required width, so two parallel faces of the work are milled simultaneously in a single pass.

q: Form milling, as carried out in a workshop, is the operation of producing:

options.A: A plain flat surface on the top of a workpiece
options.B: A slot of uniform width across a workpiece
options.C: The bore of a workpiece to a finished size with a rotating cutter
options.D: A curved or irregular profile on a workpiece, using a cutter whose cutting edges are shaped to the profile required

e: Form milling uses a cutter whose teeth are ground to the required curved or irregular profile, so the profile is reproduced on the workpiece in one pass, as in milling gear teeth and flutes.

q: Phosphating of steel components in a workshop is a surface treatment in which the components are:

options.A: Heated and quenched in oil to harden their surface layer
options.B: Given a phosphate coating by a chemical treatment, which improves the adhesion of paint and affords protection against rust
options.C: Coated with a layer of phosphate-free enamel and baked in an oven
options.D: Polished with phosphate powder to give them a bright finish

e: Phosphating chemically converts the steel surface to a phosphate coating; the coating holds and bonds paint firmly and gives protection against rust, which is why parts are phosphated before painting.

q: Powder coating of articles in the paint shop of a workshop is a finishing process in which:

options.A: A liquid paint is thinned with powder and sprayed on the article
options.B: The article is dipped in molten metal powder and allowed to cool
options.C: A dry powder is applied to the article, commonly by an electrostatic spray, and is then cured under heat to form a hard protective and decorative coating
options.D: The article is rubbed with coloured powder to fill the pores of the metal

e: In powder coating a dry powder is sprayed, usually electrostatically, onto the article and then cured by heat so it melts and sets into a hard, continuous protective and decorative film.

q: Degreasing of components in a workshop, before they are painted, coated or assembled, consists of:

options.A: Removing oil, grease and dirt from their surface, commonly by a solvent or an alkaline solution
options.B: Removing the hard scale formed on them during heat treatment
options.C: Washing off the sand that adheres to them after casting
options.D: Drying them in a hot-air oven after they have been washed

e: Degreasing removes oil, grease and dirt from component surfaces, using a solvent or alkaline solution; a clean, grease-free surface is essential before painting, coating or assembly.

q: Cylindrical grinding, as carried out in a workshop, is the grinding operation employed for:

options.A: Producing a flat surface on a component held on a magnetic chuck
options.B: Sharpening the teeth of milling cutters and drills
options.C: Grinding the inside surface of a hole or bore in a component
options.D: Finishing the external cylindrical surface of a workpiece which is rotated, commonly between centres, against the grinding wheel

e: Cylindrical grinding finishes external cylindrical surfaces: the work rotates, commonly between centres, against the grinding wheel, giving accurate size, roundness and a fine finish on shafts and pins.

q: Internal grinding, as carried out in a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Grinding the flat side faces of a component to make them parallel
options.B: Grinding the internal surface of a hole or bore with a small grinding wheel carried on a spindle
options.C: Grinding the root of a screw thread cut on a shaft
options.D: Grinding the bore of a grinding wheel before it is mounted

e: Internal grinding finishes the inside surface of a hole or bore using a small wheel on a spindle that enters the bore, producing accurate internal size and finish.

q: A chip breaker provided on a cutting tool used in a workshop is a groove, step or attachment on the face of the tool which serves to:

options.A: Conduct the cutting fluid directly to the cutting edge of the tool
options.B: Strengthen the cutting edge so that it can take heavier cuts
options.C: Break up long continuous chips into short pieces, so that they are safer to handle and easier to dispose of
options.D: Prevent the tool from digging into the workpiece at the start of a cut

e: A chip breaker is a groove, step or clamp on the tool face that curls and snaps long continuous chips into short pieces; broken chips are safer to handle and do not foul the machine or work.

q: The tool signature of a single-point cutting tool used in a workshop means:

options.A: The standardised statement of the geometry of the tool, setting out its principal angles and nose radius in a prescribed order
options.B: The maker's name and trade mark stamped on the shank of the tool
options.C: The record kept in the tool room of the tools issued to each worker
options.D: The shape given to the tool by the grinder who sharpens it

e: The tool signature is the standardised statement of a single-point tool's geometry, listing its principal angles - back rake, side rake, end and side clearance, end and side cutting edge angles - and nose radius in a fixed order.

q: The point angle of a twist drill used in a workshop is:

options.A: The angle at which the flutes of the drill are twisted along its body
options.B: The angle included between the cutting edges at the point of the drill
options.C: The angle of the web of the drill at its centre
options.D: The angle at which the drill is held to the work while drilling

e: The point angle of a twist drill is the included angle between its two cutting edges at the point, commonly 118 degrees for general work; it is not the helix angle of the flutes.

q: A boring bar used in a workshop is:

options.A: A bar of boring steel from which boring tools are ground by the fitter
options.B: A long bar used for testing the alignment of the bores of a machine
options.C: A bar which is inserted in a bore to measure its size by comparison
options.D: A rigid bar which carries the boring cutter and is fed into the work to enlarge and machine a bore, on a lathe or a boring machine

e: A boring bar is a rigid bar carrying a boring cutter, fed into an existing hole on a lathe or boring machine to enlarge the bore and machine it truly and to size.

q: Stellite, used for cutting tools in a workshop, is a tool material which is:

options.A: A grade of high-carbon steel hardened by quenching in water
options.B: A powder of silicon carbide pressed into the shape of a tool
options.C: A hard non-ferrous alloy based mainly on cobalt and chromium, which keeps its hardness at high temperatures and is cast into tool tips
options.D: A ceramic material made from bauxite for use in grinding wheels

e: Stellite is a cast non-ferrous alloy based on cobalt and chromium with tungsten; it retains hardness at red heat, so it is cast into tool tips for cutting at high speeds and on hard materials.

q: Superfinishing of a component in a workshop is a finishing process in which:

options.A: The component is finished by hand with a scraper to a bearing fit
options.B: A fine abrasive stone, given a short and rapid oscillation under light pressure against the rotating work, removes very little metal and produces an extremely smooth surface
options.C: The component is rolled between hardened plates to improve its finish
options.D: The component is immersed in a chemical bath which dissolves its high spots

e: Superfinishing runs a fine abrasive stone with a short, rapid oscillation under light pressure against rotating work; it removes only a trace of metal and leaves an extremely smooth, accurate surface.

q: Deburring of a manufactured component in a workshop means:

options.A: Removing the burrs, that is, the thin ragged and sharp edges left on the component after machining or cutting, so that it is safe to handle and fits correctly
options.B: Removing the discoloration left on the component by heat treatment
options.C: Washing the component to remove the cutting oil left on it
options.D: Testing the component for hidden cracks below its surface

e: Deburring removes the burrs - thin ragged, sharp edges raised by machining, drilling or cutting - so the component is safe to handle, assembles correctly and does not damage mating parts.

q: Cyaniding of a steel component in a workshop is a case-hardening process in which:

options.A: The component is packed in charcoal and heated for a long period in a furnace
options.B: Nitrogen alone is diffused into the surface of the component from a gas
options.C: The component is heated in a furnace through and through and quenched in brine
options.D: Carbon and nitrogen are absorbed into the surface of the component heated in a molten cyanide salt bath, producing a hard wear-resistant case

e: In cyaniding, steel parts are heated in a molten cyanide salt bath and absorb both carbon and nitrogen into the surface, forming a thin hard, wear-resistant case quickly.

q: Coining, as carried out on a press in a workshop, is a cold-working operation in which:

options.A: A hole is punched in a sheet and the punched-out piece is the article required
options.B: A sheet is bent along a straight line to a required angle
options.C: Metal held in a closed die is squeezed under great pressure so that it flows into the details of the die, giving an article of precise size and fine surface detail
options.D: A flat blank is drawn into the shape of a cup or shell

e: Coining squeezes metal in a closed die under very high pressure so it flows into the finest die details; the article gets precise size and sharp surface detail, as in coins and medallions.

q: Notching, as carried out on a press in a workshop, is the operation of:

options.A: Cutting a hole in the middle of a sheet, the piece cut out being scrap
options.B: Cutting out a portion of metal from the edge or side of a sheet or blank
options.C: Trimming the edge of a drawn cup to a uniform height
options.D: Marking the position of holes on a sheet before they are drilled

e: Notching cuts away a portion of metal from the edge or side of a sheet or blank, as distinct from piercing a hole in the middle; it prepares edges for bending and assembly in press work.

q: Eccentric turning on a centre lathe in a workshop is the operation of turning a workpiece which is mounted:

options.A: With its axis offset from the axis of the lathe spindle, so that the portion turned is eccentric to the main axis of the workpiece, as in a crankpin
options.B: In a chuck gripping it at one end only, without support at the other end
options.C: Between centres with the tailstock centre deliberately loosened
options.D: On a face plate for facing the end of a large casting

e: Eccentric turning mounts the work with its axis offset from the spindle axis, so the portion turned is eccentric to the main axis, which is how crankpins and eccentric shafts are produced on a lathe.

q: Jig boring, as carried out in a workshop, is a boring operation performed on a jig boring machine in order to:

options.A: Enlarge cored holes in large castings to a rough size
options.B: Bore the cylinders of a locomotive in position on the frames
options.C: Locate and machine holes to very accurate positions and sizes, as required for jigs, dies and other precision work
options.D: Bore a long hole through a shaft from both ends at once

e: Jig boring is done on a jig boring machine with precise coordinate positioning, locating and machining holes to very accurate positions and sizes, as required in jigs, dies and precision components.

q: A spline formed on a shaft in a workshop is:

options.A: A tapered portion at the end of the shaft on which a coupling is shrunk
options.B: A coarse thread cut on the shaft for adjustment of a nut
options.C: A semicircular pocket in the shaft in which a segmental key is seated
options.D: A series of longitudinal teeth or grooves on the shaft which engage with matching grooves in a hub, transmitting the turning effort while allowing the hub to slide along the shaft

e: A spline is a series of longitudinal teeth or keyways on a shaft engaging matching grooves in a hub; it transmits torque positively while still allowing the hub to slide along the shaft.

q: A chain block (chain pulley block) used for lifting work in a workshop is a portable device which:

options.A: Lifts a load by winding a wire rope round a drum turned by a handle
options.B: Uses an endless hand chain working over pulleys to lift heavy loads with a mechanical advantage, the load being carried on a load chain and hook
options.C: Lifts a load by the pressure of oil acting on a ram below it
options.D: Is fixed to a crane girder and travels along it with the crane

e: A chain block lifts through a hand chain worked over chain wheels with gearing, giving mechanical advantage so a heavy load on the load chain and hook can be raised by modest hand pull.

q: A tab washer used by fitters in a workshop is a washer provided with projecting tabs, and it is used to:

options.A: Lock a nut against slackening, one tab being bent against the work and another against a flat of the nut or bolt head
options.B: Distribute the load of a nut over a wider area of soft material
options.C: Act as a spring and maintain tension in a bolted joint
options.D: Seal a joint against the leakage of oil or water

e: A tab washer has projecting tabs; after tightening, one tab is bent against the work or a slot and another against a flat of the nut, mechanically locking the nut against slackening.

q: Interchangeability in workshop manufacture means the system under which components:

options.A: Are each made to suit one particular mating part and are marked to be kept together
options.B: Can be exchanged between machines of different makes without any check
options.C: Are made within specified limits, so that any one of them, taken at random, will assemble and function with its mating part without fitting or adjustment
options.D: Are manufactured in one workshop and finished in another workshop

e: Interchangeability means parts are made within specified limits of size so any part chosen at random assembles and functions with its mating part without hand fitting or adjustment - the basis of mass production.

q: Metrology, as the term is used in connection with the inspection work of a workshop, is:

options.A: The study of the composition and structure of metals
options.B: The art of hardening and tempering measuring instruments
options.C: The record maintained of the gauges held in the gauge room
options.D: The science of measurement, covering the units of measurement, the measuring instruments and methods, and the accuracy with which measurements are made

e: Metrology is the science of measurement: it covers the units and standards of measurement, the instruments and methods used, and the accuracy attainable, which underlies all workshop inspection.

q: In the costing organisation of an undertaking, an investment centre is a responsibility centre in respect of which the manager is responsible for:

options.A: The costs incurred in the centre only, without regard to its revenue
options.B: Costs, revenues and the capital invested in the centre, his performance being judged by the return on that investment
options.C: The revenue earned by the centre only, the costs being controlled elsewhere
options.D: The purchase and custody of the material used by all the other centres

e: An investment centre's manager controls costs, revenues and the capital invested in the centre, so performance is judged by return on investment, not by cost or profit alone.

q: In costing, an out-of-pocket cost is a cost which:

options.A: Involves a payment in cash, currently or in the near future, as distinct from a book cost such as depreciation for which no cash is paid out
options.B: Has already been incurred and cannot be recovered by any future action
options.C: Is charged to a job although the work on it has not yet begun
options.D: Is borne by an outside party on behalf of the undertaking

e: An out-of-pocket cost involves an actual cash payment now or in the near future, which distinguishes it from book costs like depreciation where no cash leaves the undertaking.

q: In costing and in the valuation of assets, the replacement cost of an asset or of a material means:

options.A: The price at which the asset was originally purchased by the undertaking
options.B: The amount that the asset would fetch if it were sold as scrap
options.C: The written-down value of the asset as it stands in the books
options.D: The cost that would have to be incurred at current prices to replace it with an identical or equivalent asset or material

e: Replacement cost is what it would cost at current prices to replace an asset or material with an identical or equivalent one; it differs from original purchase price, scrap value and written-down value.

q: Contract costing, as a method of costing, is the method applied to:

options.A: The manufacture of a single standard article in very large quantities
options.B: Work carried out under a contract, commonly large work extending over a long period and often executed at a site, each contract being treated as a separate cost unit
options.C: Services rendered continuously to the public over a period
options.D: Articles passing through a continuous sequence of processes

e: Contract costing treats each contract as a separate cost unit, collecting its costs to find contract profit; it suits large, long-duration work, often executed at site, such as construction and fabrication contracts.

q: Multiple costing (composite costing), as a method of costing, is the method applied where:

options.A: Several identical articles are produced together in one batch for stocking
options.B: The same article is costed again and again at fixed intervals for comparison
options.C: A product is made up of many different components, produced by different processes, the cost of each component being ascertained separately and combined to find the total cost of the product
options.D: Costs are collected process by process and averaged over the output

e: Multiple or composite costing applies where a product consists of many components made by different processes or methods; each component is costed by its own suitable method and the costs are combined for the product.

q: Quality assurance, as applied to the outturn of a workshop, means:

options.A: The inspection of the finished outturn to separate the good articles from the bad ones
options.B: The testing of a sample of the outturn in a laboratory after production
options.C: The repair and rectification of articles found defective on inspection
options.D: The planned and systematic arrangements, covering the whole process of manufacture, which provide confidence that the outturn will satisfy the quality requirements laid down

e: Quality assurance is the planned, systematic system of activities across the whole manufacturing process that provides confidence the outturn will meet quality requirements; it prevents defects rather than merely sorting them out by inspection.

q: A kanban, as used in a just-in-time system of production in a workshop, is:

options.A: A signal, commonly a card, which authorises the production or the movement of material, so that work is taken up only when the following stage calls for it
options.B: A chart on which the progress of production is plotted against time
options.C: A bin in which the material required for a job is collected in advance
options.D: A bonus scheme under which payment is made for work done ahead of schedule

e: A kanban is a signal, usually a card, in a just-in-time system authorising production or movement of a specified quantity of material; work is pulled only when the succeeding stage signals a need.

q: Under VED analysis, as applied to the material held for workshop use, the items are classified according to:

options.A: The value of the annual consumption of each item
options.B: The unit price of each item, from the highest to the lowest
options.C: The criticality of each item for production, that is, the effect on production if the item is not available when required
options.D: The speed at which each item is consumed in the shops

e: VED analysis classifies stores items by criticality - Vital, Essential, Desirable - according to the effect on production if the item is unavailable, so stock control is strictest for vital items.

q: Under the weighted average method of pricing material issued from a workshop store, the price charged for an issue is worked out by:

options.A: Taking the price of the earliest lot of the material remaining in stock
options.B: Dividing the total value of the material in stock by the total quantity in stock, the rate being recalculated after fresh receipts
options.C: Taking the price of the most recent lot of the material received
options.D: Adding a fixed percentage to the last purchase price of the material

e: Under the weighted average method the issue price is the total value of stock divided by the total quantity in stock, recalculated after each fresh receipt; issues are then priced at this average rate.

q: A double-cut file used by fitters in a workshop is a file which:

options.A: Has only a single row of parallel teeth on its face
options.B: Has two sets of parallel teeth cut across each other on its face, so that it removes metal faster than a single-cut file
options.C: Has its teeth formed as separate raised points standing out of its face
options.D: Has curved teeth running across its face from end to end

e: A double-cut file has two sets of parallel teeth crossing each other on its face; the crossing teeth break up the chip and remove metal faster than a single-cut file, suiting general work.

q: A bastard file, as the term is used for files in a workshop, is:

options.A: The coarsest grade of file made, used only for rough work on soft metal
options.B: The finest grade of file made, used only for finishing fitted surfaces
options.C: A file of a grade of coarseness between the rough and the second-cut grades, in common use for general filing work
options.D: A file having one edge left plain so that it can file into a corner without cutting the adjoining face

e: The bastard grade of file lies between the rough and second-cut grades in coarseness; it is the grade in most common general use for ordinary filing where a balance of removal and finish is wanted.

q: A diamond-point chisel used in fitting work in a workshop is a chisel:

options.A: Whose cutting edge is ground to a diamond shape, and which is used for cutting grooves and cleaning out sharp corners
options.B: Whose narrow cutting edge is used for cutting grooves for oil passages in bearings
options.C: Whose rounded cutting edge is used for drawing a drilled hole into its correct position
options.D: Whose broad flat cutting edge is used for chipping flat surfaces

e: A diamond-point chisel has its cutting edge ground to a diamond or pointed shape; it is used for cutting V-grooves and for cleaning out sharp corners and square internal angles in fitting work.

q: A cross-pein hammer used in the smithy and fitting shops of a workshop is a hammer in which:

options.A: The pein is rounded like a ball and is used for riveting and shaping metal
options.B: The pein is parallel to the handle and is used for drawing metal out in line with the handle
options.C: Both faces of the head are flat and alike, the hammer having no pein at all
options.D: The pein lies across the axis of the handle, and the hammer is used for drawing out and bending metal

e: In a cross-pein hammer the pein lies across, that is at right angles to, the axis of the handle; it is used for drawing out and bending metal in line with the direction of the blow.

q: A die stock, as used for thread cutting in a workshop, is:

options.A: A wrench with adjustable jaws used to grip and turn a tap while cutting an internal thread
options.B: The holder in which a threading die is clamped and by which the die is turned to cut an external thread on a rod
options.C: A stand in which finished dies and punches of the press shop are stored in order
options.D: A machine head which carries several dies and brings each in turn over the work

e: A die stock is the holder or wrench in which a threading die is clamped; turning the stock rotates the die over a rod to cut an external thread.

q: A taper tap, as used for cutting internal threads by hand in a workshop, is:

options.A: The first tap used in a set, having a long taper at its entering end so that it starts the thread easily and aligns itself in the hole
options.B: The last tap used in a set, having almost no taper so that it finishes the thread close to the bottom of a blind hole
options.C: A tap whose flutes are twisted in a spiral so that it drives the chips forward as it cuts
options.D: A tap with no flutes at all, which forms the thread by pressing the metal aside

e: The taper tap is the first tap of a set, with a long taper over many threads at its entering end; the gradual entry starts the thread easily and keeps the tap aligned in the hole.

q: A prick punch used by a fitter in marking out work in a workshop is a punch which:

options.A: Is used to drive out pins and rivets from their holes during dismantling
options.B: Makes a broad shallow dot at intervals along a marked line so that the line remains visible during machining
options.C: Has a fine, sharp point and is used to make small witness marks on marked-out lines and to mark centres lightly before the centre punch is used
options.D: Has a stout point and is used to make the deep conical mark from which a drill is started

e: A prick punch has a fine, sharp point for making small witness marks on scribed lines and for lightly marking centres, which are then deepened with a centre punch before drilling.

q: A swage block used in the smithy of a workshop is:

options.A: The main forging surface of the anvil on which hot metal is hammered flat
options.B: A pair of tools, held one above the other, between which a groove is formed round a bar
options.C: A block of hard steel fitted in a hole of the anvil and used as a cutting edge for hot metal
options.D: A heavy block provided with holes and grooves of many shapes, used as a support on which hot metal is bent and shaped

e: A swage block is a heavy steel block with holes and grooves of many shapes and sizes, used as a support on which hot metal is bent, shaped and grooved in smithy work.

q: Mitre gears, as used in the drives of workshop machines, are:

options.A: Bevel gears of unequal size which join shafts at an angle and change the speed between them
options.B: A pair of equal bevel gears which connect two shafts whose axes meet at a right angle, the two shafts turning at the same speed
options.C: Gears with teeth cut on a cylindrical blank which join shafts lying parallel to each other
options.D: Gears whose teeth are cut in a curve so that shafts which neither meet nor lie parallel can be joined

e: Mitre gears are a pair of equal bevel gears connecting two shafts whose axes meet at right angles; being equal in size, they change direction only and both shafts run at the same speed.

q: The involute form, as applied to gear teeth in workshop practice, is:

options.A: The straight-sided form of the teeth of a rack from which all gear teeth are derived
options.B: A cycloidal curve used for the teeth of small clock wheels and instrument gears
options.C: The curved profile given to the teeth of most gears, generated from the base circle of the gear, which keeps the speed ratio between mating gears steady
options.D: The form of the space between two teeth at the root of a gear tooth

e: The involute tooth profile is generated from the gear's base circle; mating involute teeth maintain a constant velocity ratio and tolerate small centre-distance errors, which is why most gears use this form.
